say: Welcome—today is about getting comfortable with Copilot, not getting every answer perfect on the first attempt. The four stages on screen take us from asking in Chat, through creating in our apps and catching up on messages, to workspaces and agents.

We'll try thirteen short activities, using a first prompt and a follow-up rather than watching me do all the work. Keep one habit throughout: Copilot offers a response, and you decide whether the source and wording make it usable.
welcome.ask: Which of the four stages would help most with a task you already do each week?
welcome.watch: Let the four stage cards appear before pointing to the app logos; reassure beginners that they will try the prompts themselves.

say: Before we open a message box, these four cards set the boundaries for our practice. Use only work information you're authorised to access, keep personal information about members of the public out of prompts, and follow your organisation's AI, privacy and security guidance.

The last card matters just as much as the first three: check the source information before using the result. If you're unsure whether a paragraph or file is appropriate, pause and ask me rather than pasting it to keep up.
needs.ask: What would make you pause before using an email or document in one of today's activities?
needs.watch: Pause on the public-information card; do not invite participants to share real resident or customer examples aloud.

say: Each activity gives you a route into the right experience, a first prompt, a follow-up and a check. Read the WHERE line before copying anything, because a Word activity and a Chat activity don't start in the same place.

The animation shows the clicks and prompt entry, but your own Copilot is where you'll read the answer. Send the first prompt, inspect the response, then use the second prompt to refine or question it rather than treating the picture as a worked answer.
how.ask: After copying a prompt, where will you read and verify the response?
how.watch: Point to the four numbered parts in order; distinguish the illustrative screen from the participant's live Copilot.

say: Let's start with something low-pressure: an encouraging letter from an imagined future version of you. Watch the cursor open Chat and send the prompt, then try it yourself without adding private details about your life or work.

Now send the follow-up asking what the answer was based on. The useful discovery isn't whether the letter sounds inspiring; it's recognising that this first prompt supplied no real evidence about you, so a plausible personal-sounding response is not a sourced assessment.
t1do.ask: Which part of the letter sounded personal, and what evidence did Copilot actually have for it?
t1do.watch: Wait for participants to ask the source follow-up; the animated thinking dots are not a sample Copilot answer.

say: This time we're asking about actual work rather than imagining a future, so notice the Work IQ control highlighted in Chat. With it on, send the request about your last three days of emails and Teams chats, then ask for each item's sender and date.

Open the underlying messages before accepting the priority list, and keep their contents private during discussion. If you don't have the Work IQ button, use the on-screen alternative with an authorised email and check the three-point summary against that email.
t2do.ask: Does one item's sender and date let you find the original message and confirm its priority?
t2do.watch: Offer the displayed no-Work-IQ alternative promptly; never ask learners to project their inbox or read private messages to the room.

say: The settings animation moves into Personalisation and Custom instructions, where we'll describe our role and preferred writing style. Replace the role placeholder, keep the request for plain Australian English and a short answer, then save the text.

Return to Chat and ask the follow-up about your first week using Copilot. Look at the resulting structure and language rather than assuming the preference worked merely because you saved it; a reusable style instruction is useful only when the answers actually follow it.
t3do.ask: Did the follow-up start with an answer and stay within the requested three bullet points?
t3do.watch: Stop after the Save highlight long enough for learners to replace the role placeholder, then direct them back to Chat.

say: Let's take a breath: the progress bar marks three Try Outs, and our first stage is complete. You've tried an open-ended question, a work-information question and a style preference, so the answers had quite different foundations.

There isn't another prompt to complete on this checkpoint. Think back to one answer and whether you can explain what supported it; we're carrying that checking habit into Word, PowerPoint and Excel rather than leaving it behind in Chat.
cp1.ask: Which of your first three answers had a checkable source, and which depended mainly on your prompt?
cp1.watch: Use the completed first card and highlighted next stage to orient the room; allow a brief reflection without starting another exercise.

say: Now the cursor opens Draft with Copilot in a blank Word document to build a welcome guide for a new team member. Try the prompt with its three headings, using placeholders instead of real names where appropriate.

After reading the draft, ask for the shorter checklist table with Task, Who can help and By when columns. That follow-up changes the shape without starting again, but you'll still need to check that any team responsibilities or timing are genuinely correct before using the guide.
t4do.ask: Which row in your checklist would need a real team decision before the guide could be handed to someone?
t4do.watch: Give learners time to read the Word draft before copying the table follow-up; remind them that placeholders are intentional.

say: We're taking the welcome guide into PowerPoint rather than asking for an unrelated deck. The animation types a slash and selects Team welcome guide.docx; in your own file picker, choose the document you created in Try Out 4.

Request the five-slide draft with speaker notes, then add the final slide of common questions using the follow-up. Check that the slides preserve your guide's meaning and that the suggested answers are sound; if you have no guide, the displayed alternative lets you practise a team introduction instead.
t5do.ask: Which slide or suggested answer needs checking against the original welcome guide?
t5do.watch: Pause when the file picker appears; Team welcome guide.docx is the illustration, not a required filename for the learner's own draft.

say: Download Citizen_Request_Data_Synthetic.xlsx and open it in Excel before following the cursor into the Copilot pane. We're asking for three important insights in plain English, so the task is to understand the table rather than write formulas.

Then request a chart showing the main trend and compare both the explanation and chart with the workbook. Check the figures and what the axes represent before describing a pattern as important; the supplied data is synthetic, and your own alternative table must be non-sensitive.
t6do.ask: Can you trace one insight and the chart's main trend back to the cells that support them?
t6do.watch: Confirm the workbook is open before the prompt is sent; allow time to inspect chart labels and underlying figures.

say: Six Try Outs are behind us, and the stage strip now marks creating in apps as complete. You've moved a guide into a table, a document into slides, and a data question into a chart.

Let's pause without making another file and ask whether you checked those transformations against their originals. The next stage uses conversations rather than documents, but the same issue remains: a shorter or prettier version can still leave something important out.
cp2.ask: Did a draft, slide or chart need a correction before it accurately represented your source?
cp2.watch: Point to the six-of-thirteen bar and the next Teams/Outlook stage; invite one non-sensitive example of a correction.

say: Open an appropriate busy Teams chat or channel and follow the animation into its Copilot pane. Ask for a summary of the last two days and any action items for you, then use the numbered citations to find the original messages.

Only after checking those messages should you request the short reply confirming what you'll do and by when. Read the draft as a proposed commitment, not an action already taken, and make sure both the task and timing match what the conversation actually says.
t7do.ask: Does one cited message really assign the action to you, with the timing shown in the draft reply?
t7do.watch: Ask learners to open a citation privately; do not let the reply-drafting follow-up skip the source check.

say: This Outlook example starts with a long email thread, and the cursor shows where to open Copilot or Summary by Copilot. Try the summary request and check which parts of the thread support the actions it attributes to you.

The follow-up asks for a polite reply promising a fuller response by Friday, so review that promise before keeping it. A ready-to-edit reply can save writing time, but it doesn't make the proposed deadline appropriate or remove your responsibility for the message.
t8do.ask: Would the Friday commitment be appropriate for this thread, or would you edit it before sending?
t8do.watch: Emphasise that Friday comes from the workshop prompt, not necessarily the original email; keep all real thread details off the shared screen.

say: We've reached eight Try Outs, and the stage strip highlights workspaces and agents next. Before moving on, think about the difference between reading a summary and opening the actual message that supports it.

This checkpoint is just a pause, not another task to send. If you couldn't confirm an action or deadline from the Teams chat or Outlook thread, that uncertainty matters more than how fluent the summary sounded, and it's worth keeping visible as we go deeper.
cp3.ask: What did opening an original message tell you that the summary alone couldn't establish?
cp3.watch: Let participants finish their citation checks before advancing; use the highlighted final stage to explain the change of tools.

say: Download Community_Services_Team_Notes_Today.docx and Leave_and_Flexible_Work_Procedure.docx, then follow the workspace animation and add both files. This exercise gives us a deliberately chosen set of material for a one-page summary of key points and unclear information.

Ask the follow-up to turn that summary into five questions for your manager. Check the citations against the two documents, especially where the notes and procedure leave something unresolved; a useful workspace answer should help you ask a better question, not quietly fill in a policy gap.
t9do.ask: Which manager question comes from a genuine gap or ambiguity in the two files?
t9do.watch: Verify both file chips are present in the learner's workspace; the lesson's mock does not upload files for them.

say: The cursor goes through Agents & Skills to Researcher for a public-service research question. Send the prompt requesting five sourced examples of Australian state governments using AI in the last twelve months, then replace the role placeholder in the follow-up.

Don't assume that an example is current or relevant just because the report includes it. Open its source, check the date and what was actually done, then consider whether the connection to your role is supported rather than merely an appealing suggestion.
t10do.ask: Does one example's source confirm both the claimed activity and the requested twelve-month window?
t10do.watch: Allow Researcher time to finish; do not supply imagined examples while learners are waiting for their own sourced reports.

say: Prompt Coach starts with a deliberately vague request to write an email about a change. Follow the agent selection on screen, send that request for improvement, then ask for one clear prompt you can copy and use.

Compare the revised prompt with the original and identify how the goal, context and format became clearer. If Prompt Coach isn't available, use the same requests in Chat; the skill we're practising is improving the instruction, not relying on a particular answer from the mock screen.
t11do.ask: Which missing detail about the change or audience would most improve the final prompt?
t11do.watch: Offer the displayed Chat fallback if Prompt Coach is absent; ask learners to compare prompts rather than send a real team email.

say: Choose Idea Coach and replace the bracketed example with a safe team-improvement idea, such as the suggested lunch-and-learn. The prompt asks for questions one at a time, so answer them rather than rushing straight to the summary.

When you've tested the idea through that conversation, request its strongest version in five bullet points. Notice whether the questions exposed a weak assumption or practical obstacle; this is a way to challenge your thinking, not evidence that the idea has been approved or will succeed.
t12do.ask: Which question made you reconsider an assumption in your original idea?
t12do.watch: Give the one-question-at-a-time exchange room to happen; use the on-screen Chat fallback if Idea Coach is unavailable.

say: For Writing Coach, paste one appropriate paragraph into the placeholder and ask for specific plain-English improvements. The animation shows the request being entered, while the suggestions themselves will come from your own Copilot.

Then ask for a version that's thirty percent shorter and compare it with the original. Keep the changes that improve clarity, but reject any that weaken the key message or remove an important qualification; if Writing Coach is missing, the same exercise can run in Chat.
t13do.ask: Did the shorter paragraph retain the one point your audience most needs to understand?
t13do.watch: Check that learners use non-sensitive text; encourage comparison with the original rather than accepting every suggested edit.

say: Here are the same thirteen prompt pairs we used, collected so you don't have to reconstruct them from memory. Each card separates the initial prompt from its follow-up, and the download saves copilot-try-out-prompts.txt.

Choose a pair that you'd actually like to practise again, or keep the full pack for later. These are starting instructions, not stored answers or proof that a response was checked, so bring the source-checking habit back with you when you reuse them.
pack.ask: Which prompt-and-follow-up pair will you keep for a real, authorised task this week?
pack.watch: Point out the separate Prompt and Follow-up buttons; confirm learners know the text download contains prompts, not their live responses.

say: You've explored five kinds of skill today, from asking better questions to creating, catching up and working with agents. As the recap appears, pick the one that felt useful enough to try again rather than feeling you need to remember all thirteen activities.

The three habits alongside it are the part to keep every time: open the source, use only appropriate information and make the decision yourself. You can return to the Copilot journey or Microsoft Learn from here, but leave with one practical next use and one clear check.
learned.ask: Which Try Out will you repeat this week, and what will you verify before using its result?
learned.watch: Allow a short personal commitment before showing the exit links; avoid claiming everyone has mastered every app.
